To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the blockade of GABAergic inhibition within the perifornical area of hypothalamus induces a continuous wakefulness state associated to a strong muscle tone and that this state is accompanied by an activation of neurons containing hypocretin and a deactivation of neurons containing melanin concentrating hormone.

the perifornical area is implicated in the control of paradoxical sleep and that the lack or the blockade of a strong GABAA inhibitory tone in the perifornical lateral hypothalamus is a key feature of paradoxical sleep regulation.
GABAergic control is essential for sleep regulation in the hypothalamus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the hypothalamus in the regulation of sleep and waking.
the role of the perifornical lateral hypothalamic area (PFLA) in sleep regulation and with the possible involvement of the GABAergic system in the control of this area.
the role of the hypothalamus in the regulation of sleep.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
GABAA receptor activation is necessary to maintain sleep, and GABAA receptors are necessary to induce sleep, but GABAA receptors may not be sufficient to maintain sleep.
GABAergic control of melanin-concentrate hormone-containing neurons is not involved in sleep regulation.
the perifornical lateral hypothalamus contains a GABAergic inhibitory system that is involved in the control of waking and paradoxical sleeping, but not of non-REM sleep.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GABAergic control of MCH-containing cells is important to promote waking.

GABAergic neurons in the perifornical area control the waking–sleep cycle by modulating the activity of hypocretin neurons, and that melanin-concentring hormone neurons are under GABAergic inhibition during waking and are activated during sleep.

(1) GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the perifornical lateral hypothalamic area, (2) the blockade of the inhibitory GABAergic influence induces a robust waking, (3) GABAergic neurons in the perifornichal lateral hypothalamic are active during waking, and (4) the blockade of GABAergic neurons induces a continuous waking.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the GABAergic system is involved in sleep–wake regulation and that GABAergic neurons in the hypothalamus are involved in sleep regulation.
GABAergic inhibition is necessary to maintain sleep.
the perifornical area, which contains the majority of MCH neurons, is involved in the regulation of sleep.
